chapters.title: Strategic Snapshot: The Cleared Space-Tug at the Government's Door
chapters.body:
At 6:13 a.m. Pacific time on March 30, 2026, a SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base carrying the Transporter-16 rideshare stack. Tucked inside the fairing was Vigoride 7, a Momentus Orbital Service Vehicle hosting ten payloads — the most complex manifest in the company's nine-year history. Among them: a DARPA structural-assembly demonstration under the NOM4D programme, a Space Force proximity-operations experiment, an Air Force Research Laboratory rendezvous-and-proximity-operations sensor suite, a NASA communications payload, and commercial hardware from Portal Space Systems and DPhi Space. Within hours of separation, the spacecraft had powered on, deployed its proprietary Tape Spring Solar Array, established two-way contact with the Mission Operations Center in San Jose, pressurised its water propellant tank, and fired all Microwave Electrothermal Thrusters. For John Rood, who took the helm of a scandal-ridden, founder-stripped shell company in January 2022, the launch represented the clearest proof yet that the repositioning had worked.

## Four Years of Reconstruction

The company that Rood inherited bore little resemblance to the one Mikhail Kokorich had pitched to Y Combinator investors in early 2019. Kokorich's original vision — a water-plasma space tug serving commercial satellite operators at competitive rideshare prices — had collapsed under the weight of a CFIUS national-security review, a forced equity divestiture, and a simultaneous SEC enforcement action that alleged material misrepresentations about a 2019 propulsion test. The combined settlement cost Momentus and its SPAC partner Stable Road Acquisition Corp. an aggregate $7 million; the National Security Agreement signed June 9, 2021, required Kokorich, his wife, and affiliated entities to divest 100 percent of their equity by June 30 of that year. The company listed on NASDAQ as MNTS in August 2021 without its founder, without a permanent CEO, and without a credible government customer.

Rood's stabilisation programme had three interlocking components that together define Phase 2 of the company's history. First, the CFIUS wound had to be closed completely — replacing foreign personnel, restructuring governance, and demonstrating to the Departments of Defense and Treasury that Momentus was now an unambiguously U.S. company. Second, the MET propulsion system had to graduate from an aspirational concept to a flight-proven, cleared technology: across Vigoride-5, Vigoride-6, and Vigoride-7, the thruster completed hundreds of successful orbital firings, reaching Technology Readiness Level 9. Third, a government contract pipeline had to be assembled from scratch, replacing the commercial rideshare revenues that had proved insufficient to sustain operations.

## Three Theses, One Balance Sheet

The dossier that follows examines Momentus through three analytical lenses. The first is the CFIUS recovery: whether the forced founder exit and national-security governance restructuring have produced a durable competitive advantage, or simply a compliance credential that any well-funded rival could eventually replicate. The second is the MET propulsion moat: water propellant stores safely under near-ambient conditions, offers specific impulse roughly three times that of cold-gas systems, and carries eight U.S. patents — but propulsion differentiation matters only if the company can execute missions reliably and win contracts at scale. The third is the government contract ramp: from early DARPA and NASA engagements to the January 2026 qualification as a vendor on the Missile Defense Agency's SHIELD multi-award contract vehicle, which carries a $151 billion ten-year ceiling tied to the Golden Dome ballistic-missile defence initiative.

## The Financial Equation

The numbers that anchor this analysis are unambiguous in their scale. Momentus recorded [$1.11 million in FY2025 revenue](https://investors.momentus.space/news-releases/news-release-details/momentus-publishes-letter-shareholders-highlighting-progress) — down 47 percent from $2.11 million in FY2024 — against a $30.5 million net loss and a free cash flow deficit of $23.3 million. The revenue decline reflected timing, not customer attrition: large contract awards won in late 2024 and 2025 had not yet produced earned milestone payments by December 31. Then Q1 2026 arrived. Revenue for the first quarter alone reached $3.2 million — nearly three times the full prior year — driven by DARPA NOM4D, NASA, and AFRL milestone receipts tied to Vigoride 7's successful launch operations.

| Period | Revenue | Net Loss | Cash (period-end) |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | $3.08M | — | — |
| FY2024 | $2.11M | $34.9M | — |
| FY2025 | $1.11M | $30.5M | $12.8M |
| Q1 2026 | $3.2M | — | $26.2M (Apr 23) |
| FY2026 guidance | $10.0M | — | — |

As of April 23, 2026, the company held $26.2 million in cash — up from $12.8 million at year-end following a $5 million private placement and early contract receipts — and carried no outstanding debt after retiring its last convertible-note tranche. Management's FY2026 guidance of $10.0 million represents nine times the prior year's reported revenue and, if achieved, would mark the first year in which annualised income approaches 40 percent of the cash burn rate.

The central question this dossier sets out to answer is straightforward: can milestone-based government contract revenue, growing from a $10 million FY2026 target, close the gap with a $23 million annual operating cash burn before the balance sheet requires another equity raise? Phase 1 of the repositioning — the clearance, the propulsion proof, the government door-opening — is complete. Phase 2, the revenue inflection, begins now.

chapters.title: Corporate History: From Kokorich's SPAC to Rood's Pentagon Playbook
chapters.body:
## The Kokorich Vision: Water, Plasma, and the Space-Tug Promise

Mikhail Kokorich arrived at the small-satellite revolution with more operational credibility than most founders attempting to disrupt orbital logistics. A Russian-born entrepreneur who had built Dauria Aerospace into Russia's first private satellite manufacturer beginning in 2011, Kokorich understood, at an engineering level, what the emerging rideshare era was missing: a last-mile delivery layer. SpaceX and Rocket Lab could place hundreds of satellites into a common sun-synchronous parking orbit, but operators who needed a different altitude, inclination, or precise slot had no affordable option for the final maneuver.

Kokorich co-founded Momentus in San Jose in 2017 alongside Lev Khasis, a Walmart executive, and set out to solve that problem with an unconventional propulsion concept. The Microwave Electrothermal Thruster — MET — would heat water propellant into plasma using microwave energy drawn from onboard solar arrays, achieving specific impulse performance roughly three times superior to cold-gas systems. Water, the propellant, stored safely at near-ambient pressure, eliminating the hazardous-materials handling that complicated conventional high-performance thrusters. The pitch wrote itself: a non-toxic, flight-safe propulsion architecture delivering real delta-V at a price point small-satellite operators could actually pay.

The story resonated. Momentus entered Y Combinator's Winter 2019 batch and secured backing from Prime Movers Lab, the deep-tech venture fund whose thesis centered on physics-based breakthroughs with outsized economic and societal potential. By late 2020, the company was preparing a path to the public markets through a special-purpose acquisition company, and the fundraising narrative centered on a proprietary technology that had, investors were told, already been validated in orbit.

## The SPAC and the National-Security Trap

In October 2020, Momentus announced a merger with Stable Road Acquisition Corp., a blank-check vehicle targeting the space sector. The transaction valued Momentus at approximately $1.2 billion and promised capital sufficient to scale the Vigoride orbital service vehicle into commercial production. For a moment, the deal appeared to represent exactly the kind of deep-tech success story that U.S. space-industrial-base advocates had spent years calling for.

The moment was brief. In January 2021, the Department of Defense formally notified Momentus that Kokorich's Russian citizenship — and the foreign ownership structure surrounding the company — posed a material national-security risk. The determination triggered the full machinery of the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States. On February 6, 2021, Momentus and Stable Road filed a voluntary joint CFIUS notice. The outcome left no room for compromise: on June 9, 2021, Momentus executed a National Security Agreement with the Departments of Defense and Treasury as lead agencies, mandating that Kokorich, his wife, the holding company Nortrone Finance S.A., and Brainyspace LLC divest 100 percent of their Momentus equity no later than June 30, 2021. The founder who had conceived the water-plasma space tug, raised its capital, and guided it to the threshold of a public listing was compelled to exit the company he had built within three weeks of the NSA's execution.

The CFIUS resolution cleared one obstacle and immediately exposed another. While the SPAC merger process had been underway, Momentus and Stable Road had represented to investors that a 2019 in-orbit propulsion test had demonstrated successful MET performance. The Securities and Exchange Commission concluded that those representations were materially misleading. In July 2021 the SEC charged both companies with securities fraud; both settled for an aggregate $7 million, and the settlement required significant governance restructuring — independent board oversight mechanisms, compliance programs, and other remedial measures designed to prevent recurrence. The FAA, whose authorization was required before Momentus could resume flight operations, separately conditioned its clearance on the resolution of the regulatory situation. That authorization was eventually granted, allowing the commercial program to proceed.

## Listing, Leadership Vacuum, and the Rood Appointment

The SPAC de-merger closed in August 2021. Momentus's Class A common stock began trading on NASDAQ under the ticker MNTS with a company that had survived a CFIUS-mandated founder exit, a federal securities settlement, and a regulatory flight-operations pause — all before completing a single revenue-generating mission. The leadership team that navigated those closings was interim by design; the search for a permanent chief executive capable of rebuilding institutional credibility was the company's most consequential near-term task.

The board's answer was John C. Rood, who joined Momentus in August 2021 and was formally appointed Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer on January 21, 2022. Rood brought a résumé deliberately constructed at the intersection of defense policy and aerospace commerce. He had served as Under Secretary of Defense for Policy from January 2018 through February 2020 — the principal policy adviser to Secretary Mattis, overseeing 2,100 staff, $55 billion in foreign military sales, and the full architecture of U.S. alliance relationships. Before that appointment he had been Senior Vice President for International Business at Lockheed Martin, and before that he had held senior positions at the State Department covering arms control and nonproliferation. He knew how the Pentagon bought things, who inside the acquisition system held genuine authority, and how a small company could position itself to receive national-security spending. His selection signaled, unambiguously, that Momentus's future lay in the government market rather than the commercial one.

## Survival Economics: Delisting Threats, Reverse Splits, and the ATM

The Rood era's first years were defined less by strategic ambition than by the unglamorous mechanics of keeping a pre-revenue company alive on public markets. NASDAQ's minimum bid-price and stockholders'-equity requirements triggered multiple delisting notices as MNTS shares deteriorated. The company responded with a sequence of reverse stock splits — consolidating outstanding shares to push the nominal price above the $1.00 threshold — and financed ongoing operations primarily through at-the-money equity offerings, selling newly issued shares into the open market in tranches calibrated to prevailing liquidity. These mechanisms were financially dilutive and reputationally costly, but they kept the listing intact and funded the engineering program that would ultimately matter.

Revenue during this period was sparse and structurally lumpy — a function of milestone-based government contracting rather than smooth commercial subscription volumes.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $299,000 | First operational year under Rood; inaugural Vigoride missions |
| FY2023 | $3,080,000 | Peak; Caltech Space Solar Power Project, early government payloads |
| FY2024 | $2,110,000 | Deliberate pivot away from commercial rideshare in favor of government pipeline |
| FY2025 | $1,110,000 | Trough as commercial customers were deprioritized; government contracts in formation |

The decline from the FY2023 peak was not an operational failure in the conventional sense. Rood had made a deliberate resource-allocation decision: the company's engineering bandwidth, launch manifests, and business-development cycles would be directed toward agencies — DARPA, NASA, the Air Force Research Laboratory, the Space Force — whose contracts carried multi-year payment horizons and strategic value that commercial ride-share arrangements could not match. Commercial customers offering smaller, shorter-duration engagements were consciously de-emphasized. The revenue consequence was predictable and was accepted as the price of the strategic repositioning.

## Setup for the Inflection

By the close of FY2025, the pieces assembled under Rood's Pentagon playbook were converging toward a recognizable near-term thesis. The Microwave Electrothermal Thruster had achieved Technology Readiness Level 9 — flight-proven status — across Vigoride-5 and Vigoride-6 missions. A Phase 3 DARPA NOM4D award had brought total contract value on that program to approximately $4.2 million. NASA's Armstrong Flight Research Center had contracted for a $2.5 million on-orbit demonstration of the Rotating Detonation Rocket Engine aboard a future Vigoride mission. In January 2026, the Missile Defense Agency selected Momentus as a qualified vendor for the SHIELD multi-award vehicle — a $151 billion, ten-year ceiling contract tied to the Golden Dome ballistic-missile defense initiative — opening task-order access without competitive re-solicitation.

Vigoride 7 launched aboard SpaceX Transporter-16 on March 30, 2026, carrying ten payloads including the DARPA NOM4D flight hardware, a Space Force proximity-operations experiment, an AFRL SpaceWERX rendezvous sensor suite, and a NASA communications demonstration. Q1 2026 revenue reached $3.2 million — a 786 percent sequential increase — as milestone payments began flowing from contracts assembled across the prior three years. On May 5, 2026, Rood issued full-year guidance of $10.0 million, nine times FY2025's trough. The chapter that began with a Russian founder's water-plasma dream and nearly ended in a CFIUS courtroom had arrived at something that looked, for the first time, like a credible government-services franchise.

chapters.title: Products and Platforms: Vigoride, MET Propulsion, TASSA, and the M-1000 Bus
chapters.body:
## The Vehicle at the Center of Everything

Every dollar Momentus earned through FY2025, and every dollar embedded in its $10 million FY2026 guidance, traced back to a single piece of hardware: the Vigoride Orbital Service Vehicle. Understanding the company's commercial trajectory requires a granular account of what Vigoride actually is — structurally, propulsively, and operationally — and why its architecture was designed to serve a government customer base that increasingly prizes flight heritage over specifications on paper.

The Vigoride OSV launches as a secondary payload aboard SpaceX Falcon 9 rideshare missions under the Transporter program. At separation — nominally 520 kilometers in a sun-synchronous orbit — the vehicle becomes an independent spacecraft: capable of maneuver, hosting payloads, and delivering customers to orbital altitudes and inclinations unavailable as standard rideshare stops. The bus carries more than 300 kilograms of payload capacity, a figure that positions it above smallsat dispensers and below dedicated orbital transfer vehicles, occupying a niche where mission complexity and payload mass intersect in ways that single-manifest rideshare cannot accommodate. Peak onboard power reaches 3 kilowatts, generated by the Tape Spring Solar Array — a proprietary deployable-retractable panel system whose tape-spring hinge mechanism eliminates the complex motor-driven deployment hardware found in conventional rigid arrays. TASSA's design logic was economic as much as mechanical: lower part count, simpler qualification testing, and manufacturing costs structurally below the rigid-panel incumbents.

## Microwave Electrothermal Propulsion: The Physics Argument

The propulsion system is the company's foundational intellectual property and the source of its principal competitive claim. The Microwave Electrothermal Thruster heats water propellant to plasma temperatures using microwave energy drawn directly from the onboard solar arrays. Water enters the thrust chamber, microwave energy is injected at resonant frequency, the propellant dissociates into hydroxyl and hydrogen radicals and partially ionizes, and the resulting high-enthalpy gas exhausts through a conventional converging-diverging nozzle. The physics produce a specific impulse roughly three times that of cold-gas nitrogen systems — the historical standard for smallsat attitude control — which translates into significantly less propellant mass required to achieve a given delta-v. Against chemical bipropellant systems, MET carries approximately one-third the propellant mass penalty for equivalent maneuver capacity, though chemical systems retain a thrust-level advantage for rapid orbital insertion.

The practical consequence for mission planners is a water-propelled vehicle that stores its propellant under near-ambient pressure conditions. Water does not require the pressure-regulation infrastructure, hazardous-materials handling protocols, or range-safety waivers that hydrazine, nitrogen tetroxide, or high-pressure nitrogen demand. For launch integrators at Vandenberg Space Force Base, that simplicity reduces pre-launch processing time and eliminates the category of anomaly that has grounded competitors' missions during range processing.

The MET achieved Technology Readiness Level 9 — meaning flight-proven in operational environment, not simply demonstrated in a test article — after hundreds of successful orbital firings across the Vigoride-5, Vigoride-6, and Vigoride-7 mission sequence. TRL 9 matters to government procurement officers in a specific way: it closes the question of technical risk and shifts the evaluation to schedule, cost, and mission-design fit. Momentus reached that threshold without a government SBIR funding the development path, which gives the propulsion heritage an independence that matters in source-selection narratives.

## Three Service Lines, One Bus

Vigoride supports three revenue-generating service lines that share the same physical platform while addressing distinct customer needs.

Last-mile satellite delivery is the original business model: a customer purchases a rideshare slot on SpaceX Transporter, Momentus transports the satellite as a hosted payload on Vigoride, and after orbital insertion the OSV maneuvers to a target orbit the customer specifies. The premium over direct rideshare reflects the delta-v capability to reach orbits SpaceX does not service as standard stops — specific altitudes, lower-inclination LEO slots, or retrograde configurations that require dedicated maneuver budgets. The Caltech Space Solar Power Project payload on Vigoride-5, launched January 2023, provided an early commercial reference: Caltech needed on-orbit demonstration of lightweight photovoltaic and microwave-transmission hardware under conditions replicable for a future full-scale constellation, and Vigoride's hosted-payload architecture accommodated the experiment without requiring Caltech to build and operate an independent bus.

Hosted-payload services represent the second line: customers mount experiments, sensors, communications payloads, or technology-demonstration hardware onto the Vigoride bus and operate them in LEO for the mission duration. Vigoride-7, launched March 30, 2026 aboard SpaceX Transporter-16, carried ten payloads — the most complex manifest in company history — and illustrated how hosted-payload density translates directly into revenue concentration. The manifest included DARPA's NOM4D (Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-Efficient Design) in-space structural-assembly demonstration, a U.S. Space Force proximity-operations experiment, an AFRL SpaceWERX rendezvous-and-proximity-operations sensor suite, a NASA communications technology payload, Portal Space Systems' inaugural on-orbit demonstration, and DPhi Space's edge-computing payload under a revenue-sharing arrangement. Ten payloads on a single vehicle is an operating-leverage argument made in hardware.

The third line — emerging in-orbit services, including autonomous rendezvous, proximity operations, and inspection — is the company's longest-duration growth thesis. The Space Force RPO experiment on Vigoride-7 and the AFRL sensor suite were not simply payload-hosting arrangements; they were demonstrations of Vigoride's maneuverability in the proximity regime that matters for Space Domain Awareness and eventual on-orbit servicing missions. The company has not booked material revenue from RPO services through FY2025, but the mission heritage now embedded in the SEC record provides a basis for future competitive solicitations that most competitors cannot match.

## The M-1000 Bus: Heritage Without Customers

The M-1000 satellite bus is Momentus's attempt to monetize Vigoride hardware heritage in a second product line. The logic is straightforward: a customer needing a high-power smallsat bus — capable of supporting payloads requiring up to 3 kilowatts of continuous power — can either build from scratch, purchase an unproven design, or procure a bus whose structural and power architecture has accumulated orbital hours across multiple missions. The M-1000 is positioned as the third option, targeting operators who require more power than standard ESPA-class buses provide but cannot afford the cost or schedule of a larger dedicated spacecraft.

Through FY2025, however, no material M-1000 sales had been recorded. The absence reflects a structural challenge: the customers most likely to value flight-proven heritage at scale — government prime contractors and established satellite operators — also have established bus relationships with heritage manufacturers. New entrants willing to take a risk on Momentus's manufacturing process face a sourcing dependency that the company's own filings acknowledge: specialty components for MET assemblies and TASSA structures are sourced from a limited supplier base, and the manufacturing process itself is not fully protected by the patent portfolio. The patents cover the MET architecture, TASSA deployment mechanics, and related spacecraft systems across eight U.S. grants and four international grants — but they do not extend to component manufacturing processes or supply-chain configurations, meaning a well-resourced competitor could replicate the functional design using different suppliers without infringing.

## Hosting NASA's Rotating Detonation Engine

The Vigoride-8 mission, manifested for a 2027 launch, will introduce a second propulsion technology to the platform's on-orbit record. NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center awarded Momentus a $2.5 million contract in late 2025 to host an on-orbit demonstration of the Rotating Detonation Rocket Engine — a pressure-gain combustion architecture in which a detonation wave propagates continuously around a circular combustion chamber annulus, releasing energy at pressures higher than the inlet conditions and producing thermodynamic efficiency gains impossible in conventional deflagration engines. RDRE technology has been under development at NASA, AFRL, and DoD labs for over a decade; the challenge has consistently been transitioning from ground-test demonstrations to orbital operation in a space-qualified thermal and vibration environment.

NASA selected Momentus as the host vehicle because Vigoride's power generation, structural accommodation volume, and demonstrated mission-operations discipline met the program's requirements for a Flight Opportunities demonstration. The $2.5 million contract is milestone-based, and hosting RDRE does not make Momentus an RDRE developer — the intellectual property remains with NASA and its contractor partners. What it does provide is a contract revenue stream, a deepened NASA relationship across multiple centers, and a line item in future capability briefings noting that Vigoride has hosted two distinct advanced propulsion architectures in LEO.

## The San Jose Facility

The physical infrastructure supporting all of the above consolidated in early 2026 when Momentus relocated and expanded its manufacturing operations into a new San Jose Automation and Manufacturing Facility. The facility integrates cleanroom satellite assembly areas, vacuum thruster test chambers for MET qualification, and a Mission Operations Center from which the company conducts all Vigoride spacecraft commanding and telemetry monitoring. The San Jose MOC supported Vigoride-7's post-separation checkout sequence — including solar array deployment, two-way communications acquisition, propulsion tank pressurization, and initial MET thruster firings — without requiring the company to rely on third-party ground-station infrastructure for critical early-orbit operations. The combination of cleanroom manufacturing and on-site mission operations under one roof is an operational-risk reduction argument: the team assembling the hardware is adjacent to the team flying it, which compresses anomaly resolution timelines in ways that geographically distributed operations cannot match. Specific square footage and chamber pressure specifications had not been disclosed in public SEC filings as of the snapshot date, but the facility's role as the single integration and operations hub for all Vigoride missions gives it a functional centrality that exceeds its physical footprint.

chapters.title: Financial Deep Dive: Milestone Revenue, Cash Burn, and the Path to Sufficiency
chapters.body:
|---|---|
| FY2020 | $365K | Early hosted-payload contracts, pre-launch |
| FY2021 | $330K | SPAC transition year; no orbital missions |
| FY2022 | $299K | Vigoride-5 first flight; partial milestone recognition |
| FY2023 | $3.08M | Vigoride-5 and -6 missions; first government contract completions |
| FY2024 | $2.11M | Transition to milestone-gated government pipeline |
| FY2025 | $1.11M | DARPA NOM4D Phase 3 and NASA RDRE awarded but payments not yet earned |
| Q1 2026 | $3.2M | Vigoride 7 launch milestones; DARPA, NASA, AFRL receipts |

The $365K reported in FY2020 and the near-identical $330K in FY2021 captured pre-flight deposit and service-agreement recognition from commercial operators who had signed hosted-payload contracts before the company ever reached orbit. The 2021 figure is particularly notable for what surrounds it: the CFIUS-forced exit of founder Mikhail Kokorich, the SEC settlement over the 2019 propulsion test misrepresentations, and the SPAC listing that brought John Rood into the chairman's seat. Revenue was, in that year, almost an afterthought against an existential governance crisis.

The $299K in FY2022 reflected Vigoride-5's debut flight in January of that year — a mission that demonstrated the Microwave Electrothermal Thruster at Technology Readiness Level 9 for the first time but generated only partial milestone billings as the company worked through contract structures that had not been designed for orbital execution risk. The subsequent jump to $3.08M in FY2023 was the first evidence that the government pivot was structurally sound: Vigoride-5 and Vigoride-6 missions both contributed milestone completions, and the first DARPA and NASA contracts moved from booking to cash receipt. FY2024's decline to $2.11M and FY2025's further compression to $1.11M are the numbers most likely to alarm investors scanning a summary table — but they reflect a specific dynamic in government contracting rather than customer deterioration. DARPA's NOM4D Phase 3 expansion (approximately $4.2 million total contract value) was awarded in February 2025; the NASA Rotating Detonation Rocket Engine contract ($2.5 million, Armstrong Flight Research Center) followed in autumn 2025. Neither contract had a Vigoride flight date before year-end, so neither generated material milestone revenue within FY2025. The $1.11M that did register came from earlier contract phases already in execution.

The Q1 2026 number reframes the entire sequence. Three-point-two million dollars in a single quarter — nearly three times full-year FY2025 — arrived as Vigoride 7 cleared orbital-operations milestones following its March 30, 2026 launch. DARPA, NASA, and AFRL each had payloads aboard; each had milestone structures tied to launch, separation, power-on, and initial operations. Those events occurred. The cash followed.

## The Cost Structure and the Leverage Hidden Inside It

If Momentus's revenue history is unconventional, its cost structure is almost paradoxical. In FY2025, the company reported cost of revenue of approximately $2,000 — not $2 million, but two thousand dollars — against $1.11 million of revenue. The gross margin is, in a narrow accounting sense, essentially 100 percent.

That figure is not a rounding artifact. It reflects the economic reality of milestone-based government contracts: once a spacecraft is built and launched, completing a contractual milestone — operating a hosted payload, firing a thruster on schedule, demonstrating a proximity maneuver — costs almost nothing at the margin. The spacecraft already exists. The Mission Operations Center is already staffed. The propellant was purchased at the time of spacecraft preparation. Incremental revenue from milestone certification carries virtually no incremental direct cost.

The operating cost structure is dominated instead by two fixed-overhead lines:

| Cost Category | FY2025 |
|---|---|
| Research & Development | $9.2M |
| Selling, General & Administrative | $19.2M |
| Cost of Revenue | ~$2K |
| **Total Operating Expenses (ex-revenue)** | **~$28.4M** |
| **Operating Loss** | **~$(27.3M)** |

The SG&A figure of $19.2 million — nearly seventeen times FY2025 revenue — reflects a compliance-heavy, CFIUS-regulated, NASDAQ-listed company that carries legal, audit, insurance, and executive costs disproportionate to its current revenue base. The R&D spend of $9.2 million funds Vigoride platform evolution, the M-1000 satellite bus, TASSA solar array development, and the proximity-operations and in-orbit services capabilities that management believes will define the FY2027-forward competitive position.

The leverage arithmetic embedded in this structure is striking. If FY2026 revenue reaches the guided $10.0 million with no increase in headcount or fixed overhead — a defensible assumption given management's emphasis on Vigoride as an already-built, already-staffed operational platform — the incremental $8.9 million above FY2025 falls almost entirely to operating income. An operating loss that was $27.3 million on $1.11 million of revenue could compress to roughly $18–19 million on $10 million of revenue, without a single new hire. At $20 million of annual revenue, still achievable within two years if the Vigoride 8 manifest performs, the operating loss would approach single digits. This is the financial thesis for Momentus in a single sentence: the fixed-cost base is largely already paid; the question is only whether the mission cadence arrives fast enough to outrun the cash burn.

## The Cash Bridge and the April Inflection

Momentus closed FY2025 with $12.8 million in cash and cash equivalents at December 31, 2025 — a balance that, at the FY2025 operating cash outflow rate of $23.3 million per year, implied approximately 6.6 months of runway. That figure generated legitimate concern about near-term liquidity.

The subsequent cash bridge to $26.2 million as of April 23, 2026 was constructed from two distinct sources. A $5 million private placement provided fresh equity capital without relying on the at-the-market facility — important because the ATM, while available, dilutes at prevailing market prices that had traded as low as $3.11 during the prior twelve months. The remaining improvement came from the Q1 2026 contract milestone payments: DARPA's NOM4D Phase 3 trigger events following Vigoride 7 separation and payload activation, NASA certification payments tied to the communications payload, and the approximately $1.9 million in AFRL SpaceWERX contract receipts related to the RPO sensor suite demonstration. Simultaneously, in April 2026, Momentus retired its final $1.35 million tranche of outstanding convertible notes, eliminating debt from the balance sheet entirely.

The net result was a cash position that covered operations at the FY2025 burn rate through approximately June 2027 — and materially longer if the Q1 2026 revenue velocity was sustained rather than a one-quarter anomaly. Q1 2026 operating cash outflow was not separately disclosed in the prep materials, but if operating expenses ran at approximately the FY2025 quarterly average of $5.8 million while revenue came in at $3.2 million, net cash consumption in the quarter would have been approximately $2.6 million against an opening balance of $12.8 million — consistent with the remaining $8.4 million improvement being attributable to the private placement and net contract receipts.

## Capital Structure: Dilution, Splits, and Survival

The equity base that supports the current balance sheet has been reshaped repeatedly since the 2021 SPAC listing. Momentus entered public markets with a conventional SPAC share count in the tens of millions; by May 2026, Class A shares outstanding had been compressed to approximately 6.18 million through multiple reverse stock splits executed to maintain the NASDAQ minimum bid price of $1.00 per share.

Each reverse split preserved NASDAQ listing status while arithmetically concentrating the remaining share count — the economic dilution had already occurred through the ATM equity offerings that funded operations across FY2022–FY2025. ATM programs are a standard survival tool for pre-revenue-scale public companies: the company files a shelf registration, appoints an agent, and sells shares into the open market at prevailing prices. The dilution is real but gradual, and it avoids the binary risk of a large underwritten offering that might fail to price in a volatile tape. The cost is that equity is issued at whatever price the market offers, which across a period spanning $3.11 to $43.55 on a trailing twelve-month basis creates significant variability in effective issuance price.

The $5 million April 2026 private placement at a negotiated price — executed concurrent with the convertible note retirement — was preferable to ATM issuance in that it provided certainty of proceeds at a defined price without market-timing risk. The convertible notes themselves, now fully retired, had represented a modest but real overhang: convertible debt creates dilution uncertainty and carries coupon obligations that compete with operational cash needs.

## Runway: The Model and Its Failure Points

At $26.2 million in cash and a FY2025 run-rate cash burn of $23.3 million annually, the arithmetic baseline implies approximately 13.5 months of runway from the April 23, 2026 measurement date — extending to approximately late May or June 2027. Management's own model assumes that FY2026 revenues of $10.0 million reduce cash consumption materially: if operating expenses hold flat at approximately $28 million and revenue reaches $10 million, the net cash outflow shrinks to roughly $18 million for the year, extending runway by approximately three additional months per dollar of revenue above baseline.

The $10 million guidance, if achieved, would push the runway to approximately 18–20 months from the April 2026 cash measurement — through late 2027, at which point Vigoride 8's mission completion would be expected to contribute $3–5 million in additional milestone receipts. The model threads a narrow path: it requires that Q1 2026's $3.2 million was not front-loaded and that subsequent quarters in FY2026 deliver meaningful milestone receipts. If Vigoride 7 milestone completions were substantially concentrated in Q1 and later quarters revert toward the FY2025 quarterly average of approximately $280,000, full-year FY2026 revenue would fall well below $10 million and the runway calculus deteriorates sharply.

The key failure points are identifiable and specific: a Vigoride 7 anomaly that prevents later-stage milestone certification; a Vigoride 8 launch delay beyond 2027 that pushes NASA and second-tranche contract payments out of the model window; or an unexpected step-up in SG&A from legal, compliance, or executive costs that inflates the fixed overhead base. Any one of these, unmitigated, would require an additional equity raise before the end of 2027.

## The Going-Concern Asterisk and the Threshold to Remove It

Every Momentus annual filing since FY2022 has carried going-concern language from its independent auditors — a qualification that flags substantial doubt about the company's ability to continue as a going concern for twelve months from the filing date. The language in the FY2025 10-K reflected the auditors' assessment at December 31, 2025 cash levels of $12.8 million against a burn rate exceeding $23 million annually. Management's standard mitigation disclosure in each filing has cited its ability to access the ATM equity facility, its government contract pipeline, and its option to reduce discretionary operating expenditures.

Auditors typically lift the going-concern qualification when a company can demonstrate twelve-month liquidity with reasonable certainty — typically interpreted as cash on hand plus contracted receivables exceeding the expected operating cash outflow over the forward four quarters, without reliance on speculative new raises. At the April 2026 cash level of $26.2 million and a moderating burn rate driven by FY2026 revenue, the FY2026 10-K (to be filed in spring 2027) will be the first credible candidate for a clean opinion — but only if actual FY2026 revenue lands near guidance and the balance sheet at December 31, 2026 remains above approximately $15–18 million. A revenue shortfall that pushes the year-end cash below $12 million would likely regenerate the qualification for a fifth consecutive year. The removal of going-concern language, when it comes, will be as much a market-perception event as an accounting one: for institutional investors with mandate restrictions on going-concern issuers, a clean FY2026 opinion would expand the accessible investor base in ways that no press release about a new contract award can replicate.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## A Valuation Built on Optionality, Not Earnings

Momentus presents one of the more demanding valuation exercises in the small-cap space sector. Traditional earnings-based multiples — price-to-earnings, EV/EBITDA — are arithmetically meaningless for a company that generated $1.11 million in FY2025 revenue against a $30.5 million net loss and a $27.3 million operating deficit. What the analyst is actually pricing when buying MNTS is not a stream of near-term cash flows but a staged set of binary outcomes: whether the government-services franchise inflects on schedule, whether the Vigoride mission cadence holds, and whether the regulatory moat — CFIUS clearance, U.S.-only ownership, a CEO with a Pentagon Rolodex — translates into durable contract advantage. That framing, rather than any conventional multiple, is the correct starting point.

## The Numbers on the Screen

As of the May 26, 2026 snapshot, Momentus carried approximately 6.18 million Class A shares outstanding. At the session's closing price of $15.48 — itself the product of a 110 percent single-day surge on contract-news catalysts — the implied market capitalization was approximately $95.6 million. Against a cash balance of $26.2 million (reported April 23, 2026) and zero debt following the retirement of the last $1.35 million convertible-note tranche in April, enterprise value stood at roughly $69 million.

On trailing twelve-month revenue of $1.11 million (FY2025), that yields an EV/Sales multiple of approximately 62 times — a figure that, taken in isolation, would suggest grotesque overvaluation. It is not. It reflects instead the full subordination of trailing revenue to forward expectations: the market is almost entirely pricing the FY2026 guidance of $10.0 million and, implicitly, an extended government-services ramp beyond it. On the forward revenue estimate, the picture compresses sharply. FY2026E EV/Sales of approximately 6.9 times is elevated but not indefensible for a pre-scale government-technology company with a sole-source contract pipeline, no leverage, and a demonstrated first-quarter print ($3.2 million in Q1 2026 alone) that validates the guidance trajectory.

Price-to-book offers a supplementary data point. With total assets of $40.3 million and total liabilities of $23.2 million at December 31, 2025 year-end, book value approximated $17.1 million — implying a P/B of roughly 5.6 times at the snapshot price. That premium is not unusual for IP-heavy aerospace hardware companies, where balance sheets systematically understate the value of flight-proven systems, patents, and cleared workforce relationships.

## Historical Multiple Range

The stock's five-year trading history is a compressed record of the entire SPAC era and its aftermath. MNTS listed at the completion of its Stable Road SPAC merger in August 2021, briefly trading above $10 on a pre-reverse-split basis before the SEC enforcement action and going-concern disclosures sent the share price into a multi-year decline. The company executed multiple reverse stock splits between 2022 and 2025 to maintain NASDAQ's $1.00 minimum bid price, making raw price comparisons across periods unreliable without split-adjustment. On a split-adjusted basis, the 52-week range spanning the twelve months before the snapshot was $3.11 to $43.55 — a band wide enough to render any single-point valuation observation nearly meaningless and to confirm that the stock trades primarily on sentiment, contract-news flow, and liquidity rather than on fundamental earnings capacity.

The relevant re-rating observation is directional: from a market capitalization that dipped below $20 million in distressed periods during 2024 to approximately $95 million at the snapshot, the stock has partially rehabilitated itself on the strength of the Q1 2026 revenue print and the FY2026 guidance issuance. The current implied EV/FY2026E Sales of 6.9 times represents the first point in the company's post-SPAC history where the multiple is being applied to a revenue forecast that management has substantiated with an in-quarter milestone receipt.

## Peer-Group Comparison

No listed U.S. company offers a perfect analogue — that structural isolation is partly the thesis. The closest public comps span the broader government-focused space-infrastructure category.

| Company | Ticker | Est. Market Cap | Est. EV | LTM Revenue (approx.) | EV / LTM Rev | FWD EV / Rev | Government Revenue Mix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Momentus | MNTS | $96M | $69M | $1.1M | 62x | ~6.9x (FY26E) | ~100% |
| Rocket Lab | RKLB | ~$7.0B | ~$7.0B | ~$400M | ~17x | ~11x | ~50% |
| Redwire | RDW | ~$300M | ~$350M | ~$275M | ~1.3x | ~1.1x | ~70% |
| Intuitive Machines | LUNR | ~$600M | ~$550M | ~$220M | ~2.5x | ~1.9x | ~95% |
| Planet Labs | PL | ~$400M | ~$380M | ~$240M | ~1.6x | ~1.4x | ~40% |
| Spire Global | SPIR | ~$250M | ~$280M | ~$130M | ~2.2x | ~1.8x | ~60% |

*Peer figures are estimates based on publicly available SEC filings and market data as of approximately Q1 2026; exact snapshot-date figures may differ. MNTS figures derived from primary sources as described above.*

The table makes two things plain. First, Momentus's trailing EV/Sales is a statistical outlier driven by the near-zero revenue denominator, not by a fundamental valuation premium. Second, on a forward basis (6.9x FY26E), the company trades at a meaningful premium to the Redwire / Planet / Spire cluster (1.1–1.8x forward) but below Rocket Lab (11x), reflecting the market's acknowledgement that Momentus has higher execution risk and a less diversified revenue base than even Rocket Lab. The appropriate target zone for a de-risked Momentus — one that demonstrates sustained FY2026 revenue execution and successfully manifests Vigoride 8 — would likely compress toward the 3–5x forward-sales range that characterizes Intuitive Machines and Spire, implying modest downside on the forward multiple if the guidance is met but the growth trajectory beyond 2026 remains uncertain.

## What the Current Price Implies

A simplified reverse DCF helps frame the embedded expectation. At a $69 million enterprise value, and assuming a long-run terminal free-cash-flow margin of 15 percent (reasonable for a government-technology service business at scale), the implied steady-state revenue is approximately $460 million — a level Momentus would not approach for many years even in the most optimistic contract scenario. That apparent absurdity resolves when the discount rate is adjusted for survival risk: the market is implicitly assigning significant probability weight to scenarios where the company achieves venture-style growth or is acquired by a prime contractor seeking a cleared orbital-services capability.

A more operationally grounded framing assumes the company reaches cash-flow breakeven when annual revenue covers the fixed operating cost base of approximately $28–30 million. At a gross margin near 100 percent (milestone-based government contracts carry near-zero incremental cost of revenue), that implies a breakeven revenue threshold of roughly $28–30 million. The current cash position of $26.2 million, at a burn rate declining from $23.3 million annually as contract receipts accelerate, gives approximately 14 months of runway at FY2025 burn — but more like 20–24 months if Q1 2026 contract velocity is sustained through the year.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull — $28–35 per share.** Vigoride 7 completes all DARPA NOM4D, AFRL, and Space Force milestones on schedule through mid-2026; FY2026 revenue lands at or above the $10 million guidance; Vigoride 8 launches in Q1 2027 with full manifest intact; the MDA SHIELD qualification produces the first task-order revenue in H2 2026. Under this scenario, FY2027 revenue plausibly reaches $18–22 million, annual burn narrows to $18 million, and the forward EV/Sales multiple re-rates to 5–6 times FY2027 estimates. That implies an enterprise value of $90–130 million, or a market capitalisation of $116–156 million after adding remaining cash. At 6.18 million shares, the per-share range is approximately $19–25 on mid-cycle assumptions, reaching the low $30s if institutional re-rating follows from a second consecutive year of guidance delivery.

**Base — $12–18 per share.** FY2026 revenue meets guidance at $10 million; FY2027 growth slows to $14–16 million as Vigoride 8 launch slips by one quarter and MDA task-order ramp takes longer than anticipated. The company requires one additional small equity raise in early 2027. Forward EV/Sales compresses to 3.5–4.5 times FY2027 estimates, yielding an enterprise value of $49–72 million and a market cap of $70–98 million. At current diluted shares, this corresponds to approximately $11–16 per share — broadly consistent with where the stock settled after the May 26 surge, suggesting the base case is effectively priced in at the snapshot.

**Bear — $4–7 per share.** A Vigoride 7 or Vigoride 8 mission anomaly defers material milestone payments; FY2026 revenue comes in at $5–7 million; the company executes a dilutive ATM offering at depressed prices to extend runway. Market sentiment reverts to the distressed-equity framework that prevailed through much of 2024. At 1.5–2.0 times depressed FY2027 revenue estimates of $10–12 million, enterprise value falls to $15–24 million, and the market cap declines to $35–50 million on a diluted share count that may have grown to 8–10 million shares via the offering. Per-share value: $4–7.

## The Gap Between Market and Dossier

At the May 26 snapshot, the market appeared to be pricing something between the base and the lower end of the bull case — crediting the Q1 2026 revenue inflection and accepting the FY2026 guidance at face value, but not yet pricing in a multi-year government-services franchise. The dossier's read is that this agnosticism is rational given the execution variables that remain open: Vigoride 7 milestone certification timelines, the pace of MDA SHIELD task-order conversion, and the as-yet untested repeatability of the government-contract ramp across more than one fiscal year. The structural case — cleared U.S. operator, flight-proven MET propulsion, CEO with direct Pentagon policy experience — is real. But structural cases do not generate shareholder returns until they convert into contracted revenue at a rate that narrows the gap between the $10 million guidance and the $28–30 million breakeven threshold. Until that gap is demonstrably closing, the stock deserves its current premium over book and its discount to aspirational bull-case targets in roughly equal measure.

chapters.title: Earnings Story: Quarterly Cadence, Management Commentary, and the FY2026 Inflection
chapters.body:
## The Long Descent Before the Turn

Momentus entered its earnings history as a curiosity: a SPAC-born space logistics company with a fractured founding story, a contested propulsion technology, and a national-security agreement that effectively dictated its business model. For three years after its 2021 listing, every quarterly earnings release told the same story — a company spending far more than it earned while betting that government contracts would eventually replace the commercial ride-share revenue it had originally projected.

The revenue arc from FY2022 through FY2025 traces that bet clearly. In its first full year as a public company, Momentus reported $299,000 in revenue — a number that in isolation looked catastrophic but was, in context, simply the product of a company that had launched its first Vigoride mission only in late 2022. FY2023 brought $3.08 million as Vigoride 3 and subsequent missions completed milestone deliveries. Then the trajectory reversed: FY2024 revenue fell to $2.11 million and FY2025 fell further still to $1.11 million, a 47 percent year-over-year decline that management attributed not to customer attrition but to the uneven recognition calendar of milestone-gated government contracts.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Net Loss | Key Operational Context |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2021 | $330K | — | Pre-commercial; regulatory remediation |
| FY2022 | $299K | — | First Vigoride missions; CFIUS NSA active |
| FY2023 | $3.08M | — | Vigoride 3–5; commercial ride-share peak |
| FY2024 | $2.11M | $34.9M | Pivot to government; DARPA NOM4D Phase 3 awarded |
| FY2025 | $1.11M | $30.5M | Milestone lag; Vigoride 6; NOM4D Phase 3 ramping |
| Q1 2026 | $3.2M | — | Vigoride 7; DARPA/NASA/AFRL milestone receipts |

That distinction — between a decline in customers and a delay in recognition timing — is critical to reading the Momentus earnings story correctly. The company's gross margin was notionally 99.8 percent in FY2025, because its cost of revenue that year totaled approximately $2,000. What Momentus sells to government customers is intellectual property, engineering readiness, and mission execution — assets that are already embedded in the fixed-cost base. The problem was not margin structure. The problem was that government contracts pay on milestones, and milestones arrive when missions succeed, not when contracts are signed.

## The Operating Cost Fortress

What the annual filings reveal is that Momentus sustained a roughly $27–30 million operating loss structure year after year, irrespective of revenue. In FY2025, research and development expense was $9.2 million and selling, general and administrative expense was $19.2 million — together accounting for the overwhelming majority of the $27.3 million operating loss on $1.11 million of revenue. The implied operating margin of approximately negative 2,455 percent was arithmetically startling but practically misleading: the denominator was distorted by recognition timing, not by a fundamentally broken cost architecture.

Net loss improved from $34.9 million in FY2024 to $30.5 million in FY2025, a $4.4 million reduction reflecting modest progress on discretionary cost control even as contract revenue declined due to milestone lag. Cash management through this period was the company's primary survival discipline. Momentus funded operations through a series of at-the-market equity offerings and private placements, alongside convertible notes structured with conversion features designed to preserve downside flexibility. The company executed multiple reverse stock splits across 2022–2025 to maintain compliance with NASDAQ's $1.00 minimum bid price requirement — each split a visible marker of how far the stock had fallen from its SPAC-era peak.

At December 31, 2025, Momentus held $12.8 million in cash against total assets of $40.3 million and total liabilities of $23.2 million, yielding a current ratio of 1.39. The balance sheet was not broken, but runway was constrained: at the FY2025 free cash flow deficit of approximately $23.3 million annually, the year-end cash position implied less than seven months of operations.

## The Q1 2026 Break

The first quarter of 2026 changed the narrative materially. Revenue of $3.2 million — achieved in a single quarter — exceeded all of FY2025's revenue nearly threefold and implied an annualized run rate of approximately $12.8 million, above management's full-year $10.0 million guidance. The jump represented an 786 percent sequential increase from the fourth quarter of 2025, the largest single-quarter revenue acceleration in the company's public history.

The drivers were three government contracts whose milestone conditions had been satisfied by Vigoride 7 mission operations: DARPA's NOM4D Phase 3 program, a NASA contract, and an Air Force Research Laboratory agreement. Each had been disclosed through prior 8-K filings; what Q1 2026 demonstrated was that the milestone calendar had begun to align with cash-in events at meaningful scale. For a company whose going-concern disclosures had become ritual language in each annual filing since 2022, the Q1 2026 release represented the first tangible evidence that the government-services franchise could generate revenue at a pace materially faster than the cost structure was consuming it.

Cash improved dramatically alongside the revenue inflection. As of April 23, 2026, Momentus reported $26.2 million in cash — more than double the December 31, 2025 balance. The improvement reflected both milestone receipts and a $5.0 million private placement completed during the quarter. Critically, the company also retired the final $1.35 million tranche of its outstanding convertible notes in April 2026, leaving the balance sheet entirely debt-free for the first time as a public company. The debt retirement removed both the dilution overhang of potential conversion and the structural subordination that convertible holders had held over equity investors through years of precarious capital raises.

## The May 2026 Shareholder Letter

On May 5, 2026, CEO John Rood published a shareholder letter laying out the strategic priorities management viewed as defining the remainder of the year. The letter addressed five areas central to the FY2026 thesis: completion of Vigoride 7's remaining mission phases, customer payload delivery on existing manifests, advancement of Vigoride 8 launch preparation, new contract award pursuit across the Department of Defense and civil agencies, and a deliberate posture shift toward cash preservation as the company transitioned from equity-issuance dependency toward contract-funded operations.

On Vigoride 7 specifically, Rood described the mission as having completed the operational phases triggering the milestone payments recognized in Q1 2026, and characterized the vehicle's technical performance as meeting the specifications required under the DARPA NOM4D and companion government contracts. The letter treated Vigoride 8 as the next material execution milestone: the vehicle was described as fully manifested with two NASA contracts, and Rood indicated that successful launch and milestone completion would add meaningfully to the 2027 revenue base. Depending on milestone sequencing, that contribution was characterized as capable of adding $3–5 million in incremental cash receipts in 2027 on top of the 2026 government ramp.

The guidance context was deliberate. The $10.0 million FY2026 revenue forecast assumed continued milestone execution on existing contracts and explicitly excluded new contract wins management was actively pursuing. Rood qualified the assumptions underlying the forecast: government contract milestone payments are contingent on mission success outcomes that cannot be fully controlled, and the Vigoride program had encountered technical challenges on prior missions. Management acknowledged that 2027 revenue visibility was higher than at any prior point in the company's history — because Vigoride 8's manifest was already committed — but declined to offer formal 2027 guidance pending confirmation of launch timing and manifest finalization.

## The Market's Verdict

The market's reaction to the combination of Q1 2026 earnings and the shareholder letter was dramatic. MNTS shares surged 110 percent on May 26, 2026, closing at $15.48 and lifting the company's market capitalization to approximately $95 million. The single-day move implied that prior to the release, markets had assigned near-zero probability to the government contract ramp materializing on the schedule management had described — a discount reflecting the accumulated credibility damage from three years of declining revenue and repeated going-concern qualifications.

The 52-week trading range of $3.11 to $43.55 through the snapshot date tells the broader story of MNTS as a binary-outcome security: extended periods of deep skepticism punctuated by sharp re-ratings whenever operational evidence confirmed that the government-services model was functioning as designed. At approximately 9 times FY2026 guidance revenue, the post-surge valuation was not cheap by conventional multiples — but the forward question was whether a debt-free, security-cleared orbital-services operator with $26.2 million in cash and a fully manifested next mission represented reasonable value at those levels, or whether the market was belatedly pricing in a trajectory toward commercial viability that three years of earnings releases had made it structurally reluctant to credit.

The FY2026 inflection, if sustained, would represent the first year in which annualized Momentus revenue approached 40 percent of the company's annual cash consumption — still far from self-funding, but a slope that could be modeled toward near-term break-even if Vigoride 8 performed and new award conversations converted. That shift in the probability distribution was what the 110 percent single-day move was pricing in.

chapters.title: Leadership: Rood's Pentagon Pedigree, the Interim CFO Gap, and a Defense-Heavy Board
chapters.body:
## The Hire That Signaled a Strategy

When Momentus's board convened in the second half of 2021 to fill the chief executive role, the company's predicament was unusual even by the standards of post-SPAC wreckage. Its Russian-born founder had been forced out under a National Security Agreement. The SEC had charged the company with material misrepresentations to investors. The NASDAQ listing had barely survived its first week. The technology worked — barely, provisionally, with caveats — but the business had no paying customers, no operating history under U.S.-person control, and a governance structure that had just been overhauled under federal supervision. The question was not what kind of chief executive could grow this company. The question was what kind of chief executive could make the U.S. government willing to do business with it at all.

The answer the board arrived at was John C. Rood.

Rood had joined the company in August 2021 as an advisor and transition executive; the formal appointment as Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer came January 21, 2022. The job title — combining the chairmanship with operational leadership — was itself a signal. The board was not separating governance oversight from execution. It was consolidating authority in a single figure whose biography served as a compliance document, a sales credential, and a political risk mitigation device simultaneously.

## A Career Built in the National-Security Apparatus

Rood earned a bachelor's degree in economics from Arizona State University, a credential that does not fully explain the career that followed. His professional life has been organized almost entirely around the intersection of U.S. defense policy and the industrial base that serves it.

His government career began with the State Department, where from 2007 to 2009 he served as Acting Under Secretary for Arms Control and International Security and as Assistant Secretary of State for International Security and Nonproliferation. The portfolio included the Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement framework — the legal machinery that governs logistics exchanges with allied militaries — and export-control policy for dual-use technologies. For a company whose founding CFIUS problem was precisely about foreign access to dual-use space propulsion technology, this background was directly relevant.

From the State Department, Rood moved into industry. He joined Raytheon, then transitioned to Lockheed Martin International, where he served as Senior Vice President from March 2016 through January 2018. In that role he managed business development across more than 70 countries, working the same foreign-military-sales channels he had overseen from the State Department side. The revolving-door critique practically writes itself; the strategic logic, from Momentus's perspective, is more useful. Rood knew the buyers, knew the acquisition officers, and knew the political-military relationships that determine which programs survive the budget cycle.

The capstone of his government service came when he was confirmed as Under Secretary of Defense for Policy in January 2018, serving under Secretary James Mattis until February 2020. The Under Secretary for Policy is the principal advisor to the Secretary of Defense on matters of national security strategy, force planning, and alliance management — a position that oversees approximately 2,100 personnel and, at the time Rood held it, was responsible for supervising $55 billion in annual foreign military sales. He sat at the center of DoD's institutional relationships with NATO, the Indo-Pacific alliance architecture, and the combatant commands. He also had visibility into the classified acquisition programs and threat assessments that shape defense-technology procurement priorities.

When Momentus needed to demonstrate to DARPA, AFRL, and the Missile Defense Agency that it was a trustworthy U.S. program-of-record candidate, it could point its CEO at those institutional relationships and let his biography do the opening argument.

## The CFO Gap and the Timing Problem

The executive team around Rood has been less stable. Eric Williams served as Chief Financial Officer through early 2026, providing the financial discipline narrative that underpinned the company's survival through multiple NASDAQ delisting threats, reverse stock splits, and at-the-market equity offerings. His departure created a vacancy at the most consequential moment in the company's financial history: heading into FY2026, in which Rood's May 5, 2026 shareholder letter projected $10.0 million in revenue — nine times the FY2025 figure — driven by milestone-based payments from NASA, DARPA, Space Force, and AFRL.

[Momentus IR press release](https://investors.momentus.space/news-releases/news-release-details/momentus-announces-chief-financial-officer-transition/) named Lon Ensler as interim Chief Financial Officer effective April 2, 2026. Ensler's background, as disclosed in company press releases and SEC filings, reflects finance and operational experience in the aerospace and defense supply chain, though he has not been presented as a permanent hire. The interim designation matters. A company managing milestone-payment timing with government contracting officers, negotiating the draw schedule on a $26.2 million cash balance, and potentially evaluating an up-listing or growth-equity transaction in the back half of 2026 requires a CFO with institutional credibility, not a placeholder. The gap between Williams's departure and a permanent appointment represents a governance fragility that proxy disclosures have not yet resolved.

## Paul Ney and the White House Exit

The departure that carried the most complex signaling was not the CFO transition but the CLO vacancy. Paul Ney, who had served as Chief Legal Officer and was Momentus's primary in-house expert on CFIUS mitigation, ITAR compliance, and the ongoing obligations under the 2021 National Security Agreement, resigned effective January 27, 2025. His destination: Deputy Counsel to the President for National Security Affairs and NSC Legal Advisor in the incoming Trump administration.

The dual reading of this departure is difficult to avoid. On the cost side, Momentus lost its most senior in-house counsel for the very regulatory frameworks — CFIUS, export control, government-contract compliance — that define the company's competitive moat and its legal obligations. The NSA executed in June 2021 remains an active compliance instrument; the ITAR frameworks governing the MET propulsion technology require continuous monitoring; and the company's increasing penetration of classified or sensitive-compartmented defense programs creates incremental legal complexity that outside counsel handles less efficiently than an embedded CLO. As of the snapshot date, the CLO position had not been publicly filled.

On the opportunity side, a former CLO now serving as NSC legal counsel represents an unusual relationship asset for a company pursuing government contracts. Ney's departure is not a consulting engagement — he moved into a principal government role — but the institutional knowledge he carries about Momentus's capabilities, compliance posture, and technology roadmap does not disappear. The company has not characterized this as a business-development advantage in its public disclosures, which is the appropriate posture, but sophisticated observers of the government-contracting ecosystem will note the circumstance.

## The Board: Seven Directors, One Thesis

The [2025 DEF 14A proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001781162/000114036125034316/ny20051539x4_def14a.htm) filed ahead of the May 19, 2025 annual meeting presents a board of seven directors constructed to solve one problem: demonstrating to the U.S. government, to CFIUS, and to institutional investors that Momentus is, unambiguously, a U.S.-controlled national-security-aligned enterprise. The average tenure of approximately 4.2 years reflects the post-SPAC board rebuild; most of the current directors arrived in 2021 or 2022 as part of the governance restructuring required under the National Security Agreement and SEC settlement.

The board's professional affiliations read as a who's-who of the defense-industrial complex. Directors carry backgrounds spanning Lockheed Martin and Raytheon alumni networks, DoD policy functions, International Space Station program management, and national-security advisory roles. Committee assignments — Audit, Compensation, and Nominating/Governance — follow standard independent-director architecture, with the Audit Committee carrying particular weight given the company's history of SEC enforcement and the ongoing complexity of milestone-based revenue recognition under government contracts.

The defense-contractor network embedded in the board creates both a channel-sales opportunity and a disclosure dynamic worth monitoring. Directors with current advisory or board relationships at prime contractors — Lockheed, Raytheon, Northrop, Boeing — or at government integrators working MDA and AFRL programs represent potential conduits for Vigoride to be embedded as a subcontract line item within larger program awards. That structural advantage has not yet been quantified in disclosed contract wins, but it represents the board's latent commercial function beyond governance.

## Compensation Architecture and Dilution Arithmetic

Rood's compensation structure, as disclosed in successive DEF 14A filings, reflects the constraints of a small-cap company with a sub-$50 million market capitalization and significant cash-burn pressure. Base salary is below the competitive market for a CEO managing a NASA and DoD contractor portfolio, a deliberate tradeoff for equity alignment. Annual incentive targets are tied to operational milestones — launch execution, government-contract awards, and cash-management metrics — rather than revenue, which is appropriate given the lumpiness of milestone-based government payments but creates incentive misalignment in years where revenue recognition lags contract awards.

The equity program — options and RSUs granted over Rood's tenure since January 2022 — has a dilutive impact on the approximately 6.18 million shares outstanding (post-reverse-split) that is material relative to the float. Executive equity grants at post-SPAC small-caps with compressed share counts routinely represent 3–8 percent of fully diluted capitalization per annual grant cycle; at Momentus's share count, even modest RSU grants visible in the proxy represent meaningful dilution for a company that has already conducted multiple reverse splits to maintain NASDAQ compliance. Shareholders evaluating the FY2026 revenue inflection story must weight milestone-payment upside against the equity-issuance cadence that funds the executive team holding those relationships.

## Key-Person Concentration: The Rood Premium and Its Risks

Every government-contract announcement Momentus has issued since 2022 carries, implicitly, the same subtext: this award was made possible, in part, because John Rood could walk into the right building and have the right conversation. The DARPA NOM4D win, the AFRL SpaceWERX engagement, the Space Force hosted-payload relationship, and the MDA SHIELD qualification all reflect a contracting dynamic in which the CEO's personal credibility with program officers and acquisition executives reduced the transaction costs of a yes decision.

The company's SEC filings acknowledge this concentration risk in standard key-person language, but the acknowledgment understates the structural dependency. Momentus does not yet have a second executive — or a board member — whose relationships with DoD, NASA, and the intelligence community are independently sufficient to sustain the government-contracting franchise if Rood departs. Succession planning disclosure in the 2025 proxy is formulaic rather than substantive. The board has not disclosed contractual retention provisions beyond standard equity-vesting schedules, which vest over time rather than conditioning retention on specific contract-renewal milestones.

The bet Momentus made in January 2022 — that a cleared, policy-credentialed chief executive could unlock government orbital-services revenue that an engineering-first management team could not — has produced measurable results by 2026. The residual question is whether the company has used the four-year Rood stabilization period to institutionalize those relationships into program-of-record status, or whether the government-contracting franchise remains a function of one executive's Rolodex. At $10 million in projected FY2026 revenue against a $23-plus million annual cash burn, there is not yet enough margin to answer that question with confidence.

chapters.title: Customers and Markets: Government Mission Pipeline from DARPA to the Golden Dome
chapters.body:
## A Customer List Built in Washington, Not Silicon Valley

When John Rood published his shareholder letter on May 5, 2026, the phrase that stood out was not the revenue guidance itself but the roster of names behind it. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center. Air Force Research Laboratory. U.S. Space Force. Missile Defense Agency. The five-line government customer list read less like the customer table of a venture-backed commercial-space startup and more like the cover sheet of a Pentagon budget justification document — which, in substance, is precisely what Momentus had become.

The company's FY2026 revenue guidance of $10.0 million, representing a ninefold increase over FY2025's $1.11 million, rested almost entirely on milestone-based payments from those five agencies. Q1 2026 revenue of $3.2 million — already three times full-year 2025 — was driven by DARPA NOM4D, NASA, and AFRL contract milestone completions tied to the March 30, 2026 Vigoride 7 launch. The commercial segment existed, but it was not carrying the financial story.

## DARPA NOM4D: The Anchor Contract

The largest and most strategically resonant government relationship was the DARPA Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-Efficient Design program, known by its unwieldy acronym NOM4D. DARPA structured NOM4D to address a problem that has constrained military and civilian space architectures since the beginning of the Space Age: the practical impossibility of launching large, rigid structures aboard any existing rocket. Communications apertures large enough to support high-gain directional links, radar arrays with meaningful cross-section, solar-power structures that could feed substantial onboard power — all of these require spatial scales that fairing geometries prohibit. NOM4D's program goal was to demonstrate that robotic assembly of large structures could be performed in orbit, decoupling deployed aperture size from launch-vehicle constraints.

Momentus entered the program in Phase 1, accumulated flight-test experience through Phase 2, and in February 2025 was awarded Phase 3, bringing the total contract value to approximately $4.2 million. The Vigoride 7 mission, launched March 30, 2026 aboard SpaceX Transporter-16, hosted the NOM4D flight demonstration hardware as a hosted payload. Momentus's role was not to perform the assembly operations itself — that was the DARPA prime's task — but to provide the orbital platform, on-orbit operations support, and the stable, power-rich environment that a structural-assembly demonstration requires. Vigoride 7's Tape Spring Solar Array generated up to three kilowatts of peak onboard power, a meaningful figure for a small-satellite bus supporting precision-pointing experiments.

The DoD interest in NOM4D extended well beyond academic curiosity about orbital manufacturing. Large deployable structures are directly relevant to Space Domain Awareness, persistent wide-area communications for joint all-domain operations, and the proliferated-LEO ISR architectures being developed across the intelligence community. A successful NOM4D flight demonstration on Vigoride 7 would advance the Technology Readiness Level of in-space assembly from laboratory validation toward operational prototype — and position Momentus as a recurring host platform for whatever comes next in DARPA's space-structures research agenda.

## NASA: Six Contracts and an Engine That Detonates

NASA's relationship with Momentus had deepened considerably by the snapshot date. The headline was a $2.5 million contract awarded by NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center in September or October 2025 to conduct an on-orbit demonstration of a Rotating Detonation Rocket Engine — a propulsion concept that, if validated at orbital scale, would represent a significant departure from conventional continuous-combustion rocket engines.

A Rotating Detonation Rocket Engine operates on a fundamentally different thermodynamic cycle from conventional liquid-propellant engines. Rather than burning propellant in a steady deflagration, an RDRE sustains a detonation wave that rotates continuously around an annular combustion chamber. The thermodynamic efficiency of a detonation cycle is theoretically superior to deflagration, and early ground-test results had suggested substantially improved specific impulse for a given propellant load. NASA's interest in an on-orbit demonstration — designated the Juno RDRE — reflected both the Flight Opportunities Program's mandate to mature novel propulsion technologies in space and the civil-space community's broader appetite for higher-performance in-space propulsion. Vigoride 8, fully manifested for a 2027 launch, would host the Juno RDRE payload, extending the NASA revenue line at least through that year. The company had described the RDRE award as the sixth NASA contract won in recent months, suggesting a systematic broadening of the relationship across multiple NASA centers and program offices.

## AFRL, Space Force, and the Proximity Operations Premium

The Air Force Research Laboratory's SpaceWERX unit represented a third distinct government revenue stream. SpaceWERX had engaged Momentus to develop and integrate a rendezvous-and-proximity-operations sensor suite, a capability set with direct relevance to Space Domain Awareness and the emerging U.S. military interest in robotic servicing and inspection of on-orbit assets. Approximately $1.9 million in contract payments were received jointly from AFRL and NASA in January 2026. Separately, the U.S. Space Force manifested hosted payloads on Vigoride 7 for proximity-operations testing — experiments relevant to both offensive and defensive Space Domain Awareness missions that the Space Force had been publicly developing since its establishment in 2019.

The overlap between DARPA's NOM4D structural-assembly work, AFRL's RPO sensor suite, and Space Force's proximity-operations experiments was not coincidental.
